item.title: The Daily Star – The unspoken and misheard
item.description:
There’s a curious paradox in fiction’s representation of childhood violence. Produced by an adult author, the text reconstructs the idea of a childhood only children can experience. And when that childhood is marked by trauma, violence, and a deliberate obscuring of the traumatic event, such portrayals raise complex questions about fiction’s complicity in narrating traumatic childhood and its aftermath. Are children’s voices ultimately protected in such narratives? 

Take Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s Half of a Yellow Sun (Knopf, 2006), where during the Nigeria-Biafra war, the readers must confront the violent transition of Ugwu, the gentle village boy who has so far acted for the readers as one of the primary anchors of the sprawling story. As a conscripted soldier, Ugwu not only blurs the line between combatant and civilian, but he also participates in the gang rape of a young bar girl. Driven partly by the pressure to conform to the codes of soldiering and a masculinised form of wartime camaraderie, Ugwu shifts from a soft and caring young boy to a violent sexual assaulter, exposing the brutal nexus of violence, gender, and war. Elsewhere in the novel, his sister Anulika too is raped by Nigerian soldiers, further amplifying Ugwu’s sense of shame and guilt. Adichie’s decision to demonstrate the violence of war through a character we had by then come to love makes explicit the unforgiving nature of war and how the sexuality of the young is viciously altered during such moments of exception. 

A more quotidian, commonplace form of sexual violence during moments of heightened political crisis is visible in Bapsi Sidhwa’s Cracking India (Milkweed Editions, 1991). The eight-year-old Parsee narrator who suffers from polio, Lenny loses her innocence right alongside India’s own loss of its self as communal violence escalates during the 1947 Partition. But it is the casual, almost offhand ways in which sexual abuse is depicted in the novel that disturbs the reader. There is the cook in the affluent Sethi household who likes to caress “soft things” like cats and children. There is Lenny’s ‘Cousin’ who, a child himself, forcibly kisses Lenny, asks her to do more. Lenny sometimes relents, other times resists. Children are married off, made to witness adult sexual encounters, all of which lend an air of normalcy to the sexualisation of minors. Lenny in particular, remains sexualised throughout—as the “queer” eye that gazes at the bodies of her mother and Ayah and as the narratorial voice demonstrating routine gendered violence that pervades the novel and—as my students remind me when we read the text in class—the regular South Asian household. 

Such shattered, fractured lives of child(ren) narrators appear in Tahmima Anam’s Uprising (Scribner, 2026) too, where the haunting tale of an island occupied entirely by prostitutes is told from the perspectives of their children. Anam’s modes of articulating the island’s ecosystem and the exploitations the women undergo testify to the brand of extraction and profiteering that is the hallmark of colonialism. The symmetrical, parallel depiction of the sites—the topological body of the island and the medicated, drugged up bodies of the women—are sites of consumption. On the island, the female bodies exist primarily in service of men who extract pleasure from their bodies. The children born on the island are neglected—the men bear no responsibilities; the mothers find them burdensome. The collective narratorial voice of the children, especially the dramatic “Oh Ma go” and “Ma go Ma” however, feels disconcerting, almost eerie. The lamentations for me, don’t adequately capture the scale of the children’s trauma—their longing for their mothers, for love, for care. With the exception of the temporary, utopian aftermath of an “uprising” in the island, the children’s trauma remains on the hem of the narrative.

Parental complicity in facilitating or ignoring the violence befalling their children remains a recurring trope in fiction set during times of intense, exceptional political upheaval. Think for instance, the much-debated final sacrifice of Buri in Selina Hossain Hangor Nodi Grenade (Anannya, 2005) where the mother sacrifices her deaf and mute son to protect the lives of the freedom fighters during the 1971 Liberation War. The sacrifice of Raees not only upholds the grand narrative of valor endemic to the nationalist mission of 1971 but also creates a rupture in our conventional understanding of maternal instinct and protectiveness. In making the choice in who gets to live, what life is livable and what life expendable, Hossain’s fictional account based on a true incident gives credence to what Nayanika Mookherjee terms the “aesthetics of nationalism”. The willful death of the disabled child in order to protect the life of the able-bodied men signifies the nationalist need to protect the “healthy” son of the soil and sacrifice the “unhealthy” body of the subaltern subject. 

Children’s sexuality and unaddressed sexual abuse are enduring plot points in Humayun Ahmed’s work. Across his impressive oeuvre, Ahmed often writes about impressionable, stunningly beautiful young girls hopelessly in love with much older male characters. In his Amar Ache Jol (Anindya Prokashon, 1985), 15-year-old Dilu commits suicide after she falls for the 35-year-old Jamil, the novel ending with her body floating in a pond in a poetic, beautiful Ophelia-esque manner. In Debi (Oboshor Prokashoni, 1985) and “Jin Kofil” respectively, Ranu and Latifa—both young women, both at the center of some mystical, mystifying ill only Misir Ali can solve—concretise Ahmed’s penchant for centering narratives around impossibly beautiful young girls, whose sexuality remains either under the secretive wraps of middle class sensibilities Ahmed has been so deft at portraying or where the women feel ashamed for experiencing even the slightest hint sexual desire. Ranu’s childhood abuse is presented in the narrative with the air of a mystical reawakening. She believes the deity of the temple where she experienced the abuse “went inside her”, allowing her to become beautiful, allowing her to become the titular “debi”. Latifa however, falls for the Imam who worked for her affluent household and the shame of falling for a man belonging to the underclass so traumatised her that she becomes a ‘monstrous mother’ herself—one who kills her own children. Such casual misogyny in the hands of one of our most celebrated and beloved writers therefore bring home the central question I have been trying to trace in this essay—that of ambiguous, complex authorial intent, and of young voices being subsumed by other, grander narratives of war, destruction, and sexual politics. 

From narratives that demonstrate the devastation children and young individuals face physically and psychologically to the constructed ideas of what children should be or sound like, from how children’s sexuality, sexual encounters, and violences are depicted to how children cope with a traumatic aftermath—literatures about children and violence rest on an aenigma—adult voices sometimes amplify their voices, sometimes obtrude them, and other times coerce them into speaking. What we make of their speech remains the task of the reader. 

Dr Nazia Manzoor teaches English at North South University. She is also Editor, Star Books and Literature. Reach her at [email protected].

item.title: The Daily Star – Mahasweta Devi on literature, resistance, and the marginalised
item.description:
Author and academic Subhoranjan Dasgupta knew Mahasweta Devi closely. She gave him what would become her final interview before falling seriously ill. In this impassioned conversation, the acclaimed writer and tireless social activist, recipient of prestigious honours including the Ramon Magsaysay Award and the Jnanpith Award, reflects on her literary creativity, political convictions and lifelong commitment to marginalised communities.

In your very first book, Jhansir Rani (1956), you departed from the typical biographical format, which might have presented her as a romantic figure.

Yes, I broke new ground. My book was not a biographical novel in the accepted sense of the term. On the contrary, I depended on meticulous historical research rooted in that region and in the imagination of the common people, particularly villagers. I examined local ballads and folklore and engaged in long interactions with local people who searched their memories to recall the queen as she had been remembered across generations. The result of this grassroots exploration was the production of a ‘human history’ centred on the queen, as recollected and retold by the people themselves.

You followed the same method in later masterpieces, too, such as Aranyer Adhikar (1977) and Titumeer (1998).

Yes. I tried to create a form of historical fiction in which the emphasis is on the revolt of the downtrodden and the exploited, be it under the great Muslim peasant rebel Titumeer of Bengal or under Birsa Munda, the tribal leader, in Jharkhand (then Bihar).

I confess I have a special weakness for Aranyer Adhikar because there I tried to interweave two layers of narrative: documentation and fearless battle. We have to admit that the conventional historiography of our freedom movement has not given the Santhals the respect they deserve for their rebellion against ruthless colonial exploitation. I wanted to fill this unpardonable gap, and what helped me immensely was my first-hand knowledge of the region and my intimacy with the local people. Once again, their memories, folk ballads and, in short, their many-faceted invocation of the past ‘humanised’ my narrative.

You are perhaps the only Indian author of our times who has consciously immersed herself in the lives of rural people and tribal communities, exploited, cheated and impoverished at every step, yet so vibrant. This was not the occasional foray of an urban intellectual but a lifelong passion. Can you explain this deliberate choice?

I cannot explain it. I can only say that I made a choice. I ignored the mainstream and I opted for them. I did not go to the Ganga and Jamuna; I went to the unknown hills and rivers deliberately. And do you know what I discovered? The great respect and love the Adivasis aroused in me! Let me say in all candour that the tribal societies of our country are more civilised, more knowledgeable and even more sophisticated than those who inhabit our metropolises. I went to them to seek inspiration.     

In the process, you came very close to the Lodhas, Sabars and other tribal communities. Did this intense engagement reduce your creative output?

Tell me, who measures the genuine worth of creativity by quantity? Many urban writers are churning out thousands of books every year on the petty trials and travails of the middle class. Don’t we consign this abundance to oblivion?

On the contrary, my social activism has deepened my experience, giving it concrete, existential shape, and defined the nucleus of my commitment. This valuable experience is layered with the invocation of myths, legends, folktales and collective memory. In short, magic realism. When you read Bashai Tudu (1978), the mysterious story of a Naxalite who revives miraculously after every encounter that riddles him with bullets, as if he were deathless.

Are you the only one in contemporary Bengali literature who has transcribed the experience of the ‘wretched of the earth’ into literary texts?

I need to correct a possible erroneous impression that only I have concentrated on the marginalised and the lowly. In West Bengal, powerful novelists like Debes Ray and Amiya Bhushan Majumdar, who were never popular in the conventional sense of the term, have also traversed the same tormented terrain. For example, Debes Ray’s magisterial Teestaparer Brittanto (1988) is devoted to the subalterns, their woes and their struggles.

Similarly, in Bangladesh, Hasan Azizul Huq, probably the most forceful short-story writer of our time, and novelists like Shaukat Ali and, above all, Akhtaruzzaman Elias have highlighted, with rebellious rigour, the deprivation and resistance of people condemned to the lowest rungs of society in towns and villages. In fact, I would like to salute Elias as the greatest novelist of our day, the very best after Manik Bandopadhyay. Believe me, he has attained this exemplary status in both Bengals by writing just two novels. Elias has proved that it isn’t quantity that matters, but quality, dedication and commitment.

I would also like to stress that our literary movement, limited though resolute, has received due recognition. Renowned directors have turned our texts into stirring plays and films, though we have never craved the applause of millions. Usha Ganguli’s marvellous dramatisation of Rudali, in Hindi, was hailed as a landmark production in West Bengal. Elias’s epic-like Khowabnama (1996) and Chilekothar Shepai (1986) were staged in both Dhaka and Kolkata with marked enthusiasm. Last but not least, my Hazar Churasir Ma (1974) inspired Govind Nihalani to create the moving Hindi film Hazaar Chaurasi Ki Maa (1998). The oppressed and erased, in short, the subalterns, won the recognition they deserve: a solemn acknowledgement, neither cheap nor tawdry.
By the way, I was extremely close to Elias. His wife, Suraiya, described our relationship most suitably. She said, “You, Didi, and my husband remind me of Apu and Durga in Bibhutibhushan’s immortal Pather Panchali.”

You are a committed Leftist, but what sort of Leftism appeals to you? Do you feel closely attached to any particular party?

You have asked a delicate and difficult question, but I shall answer it. You know that I come from an illustrious Leftist, or rather Communist, background. My father, Manish Ghatak (pseudonym ‘Jubanashwa’), was a rebel poet of sorts. My uncle was the filmmaker Ritwik Ghatak, whose adherence to Marxism calls for no special mention. And my first husband, the famous dramatist Bijan Bhattacharya, heralded the new movement of Bengali drama by writing Nabanna (1944) in the glorious days of the IPTA (Indian People’s Theatre Association).

When I dwell on this background, I find that our official Communist movements have not been able to address the burning questions of our country and society. They have become far too ‘parliamentarised’, and this tendency partly explains why I wrote Bashai Tudu (1990) and Hazar Churasir Ma (1974), two creative texts that uncompromisingly expose the brutality of the state machinery. Does this mean that I regard the extremist Naxalite movement as the only answer? Not at all. I expose the sheer mercilessness of the state and call for a system that will not provoke desperate young men to take up guns. The logic is clear. If the state adopts even minimal welfare measures that would help the poorest, the tide of resistance will ebb. But if this deprivation and persecution persist without any relief, the people will rebel in a way of their own choosing. Then, please do not blame them. The onus lies with those who govern. That is the message I wanted to convey in Bashai Tudu (1990) and Hazar Churasir Ma (1974).

I myself have adopted the constitutional route and opposed the death penalty for several extremists. My appeal was explicit in my letter to the President of India: “In the land of Buddha, Mahavir and Gandhiji, let it not be said that there is no place in our hearts for mercy.” I remain a Leftist, an ardent one. I am still searching for an appropriate path to human and social deliverance.

And this aspired-for deliverance focuses inevitably on the emancipation of the tortured, tormented Indian woman. I am referring here to characters in Rudali (1979) and Gohumani (1993). Of course, women fight against semi-feudal, patriarchal oppression, particularly in villages, because they have to live and win. Live, not just survive. I have a special weakness for Gohumani. Though bonded labour was abolished by law in 1976, it continued to survive in Palamau in Jharkhand. In 1979–80, when the bonded labourers began their fight, I joined them. Gohumani is an outcome of that actual experience and struggle.

What surprises you most?

You know, I have lashed out against the powers that be without mincing words. For example, I opposed the CPI(M) regime tooth and nail during the Nandigram tragedy. But still, God knows why, the rulers choose me as their country’s voice. Why? I was requested to lead the Indian delegation to the 2006 Frankfurt Book Fair, where India was honoured as the partner country. You know what I said in my inaugural address? “My country, torn, tattered, proud, beautiful, hot, humid, cold, sandy—my country.”

Subhoranjan Dasgupta is an academic and author.

item.title: The Daily Star – On inheriting curiosity: Notes from reading ‘For the Love of Stories’
item.description:
The older I grow, the more I realise that environments shape us long before ambition does. We celebrate extraordinary individuals while overlooking the ecosystems that nurture them. We praise the writer without noticing the childhood that taught her to ask questions. We admire the scholar while forgetting the parents who answered one question with three more.

Reading Wendy Doniger’s For the Love of Stories (Speaking Tiger Books, 2026) brought me back to that distinction. Her memoir dwells sentimentally on childhood and reveals how profoundly our intellectual lives are shaped before we begin to call them intellectual. 

We often talk about books that change our lives. We talk far less about the homes that make those books possible.

There is something disarming about the way Wendy Doniger writes about herself. item.title: The Daily Star – When Aldous Huxley’s final day mirrored his fiction
item.description:
At half past noon on November 22, 1963, a presidential motorcade drove through Dealey Plaza in Dallas, and by one o’clock, President John F. Kennedy was dead. The news was everywhere within hours. Television stations dropped everything else, and three days later, the funeral was broadcast around the world.

You didn’t have to be American, or old enough to have been in Dallas that day, to know this. It’s been sixty-odd years since, and the documentaries and conspiracy theories still run amok. A film about the assassination even has two Oscars under its belt. And you could Google the words ‘Zapruder film’ right now and find videos about it from two months ago. In the sixty-odd years since, November 22 has become more than just a date. The JFK assassination has carved out an enduring afterlife in popular culture.

The trouble with something like this is that it drowns out everything else that happened outside of it. And plenty did, in fact, happen on the same day. In Oxford, C. S. Lewis died at home, a week short of his sixty-fifth birthday. And in another home in Los Angeles, at 5:20 that same evening, Aldous Huxley also drew his last breath, while most people were glued to their televisions watching the Kennedy assassination coverage.

If you know anything about Aldous Huxley, you almost certainly know about Brave New World (1932), and if you’ve read Brave New World, you know about soma. Brave New World is set in London in the year 632 After Ford, named after Henry Ford of automobile fame. This world has swapped out God for Henry Ford, and babies are decanted from bottles at the Central London Hatchery and Conditioning Centre. They are sorted into castes, from Alphas to Epsilons, and taught in their sleep to love the lives they’ve been assigned. In Huxley’s World State, no one is lonely, nobody grieves and nobody stays angry longer than it takes to swallow one tablet. As the slogan goes, “A gramme is better than a damn.”

By this point, Huxley had spent years battling throat cancer and had lost his voice by November 22, 1963. He communicated with the people around him by writing on a notepad. At one point that morning, he handed a note to his wife that said, “LSD, 100 µg, intramuscular.”

In Brave New World, the state’s dying are sent to the Park Lane Hospital, where a television box sits at the foot of every bed and soma ensures that nobody is fully conscious of the end. Children are brought in for ‘death-conditioning’ and handed chocolate éclairs; they grow up thinking of the end of life as a treat. No one in the World State is encouraged to look death in the eye. The televisions blaring throughout the day help make sure of it.

In Huxley’s bedroom, his wife, Laura, gave him the injection and then a second dose. She sat beside him, telling him to go “…into the light, into complete love”, while elsewhere in the house, the nurses and doctor watched the Dallas coverage on television. The scene bears an unsettling resemblance to the world Huxley had imagined, where screens offered a distraction from death even as it unfolded nearby. By 5:20 that evening, he was dead.

Kennedy’s death inspired films, conspiracy theories and decades of public fascination. It almost immediately became public property and continued to occupy a prominent place in the pop-culture lexicon. Huxley’s death, meanwhile, became the third entry on a list of notable people who died that day, something like a fun fact whenever the Kennedys were brought up. The man who wrote the most famous story about complacency through distraction died while the world was distracted. In a novel, an irony as neat as that would be considered too on the nose.

And I wonder if Huxley would have recognised the joke. He had, after all, written it first.

Arshi Ibsan Radifah is a Literature major who loves unreliable narrators and Wes Anderson movie sets. If she had it her way she would have liked to play bass for a girl band in the 90s, but for now she’ll suffice by rewatching Empire Records.

item.title: The Daily Star – The goat and its geometric knowledge
item.description:
The fear of mathematics has reached almost supernatural proportions among school students in our country. Geometry is an integral component of maths. So, deductive reasoning reveals the equation:

Fear of geometry = Spectrophobia

Sri Hiralal Mukherjee (HM) taught us mathematics in class eight. He was an expert headmaster in this much-dreaded academic subject. Maths, to many of us, was as dry as hardwood. But HM sir was a pedagogic magician who knew the alchemy of transforming a sapless subject into something like an enchanting fairy tale. The hallmark of his teaching was his abundant use of unfailing humour. So, in a typical Hiralal geometry class, learners chuckled and giggled, and often enjoyed spontaneous gales of laughter.

One day, Hiralal sir drew a triangle on the blackboard and said, “The sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is always greater than the length of the third side.”

With ample illustrations on the board, he proved that the sum of the lengths of sides AB and BC was greater than that of AC. Likewise, he showed us that BC and CA together were greater in length than AB. After explaining the Triangle Inequality Theorem, HM hurled his terrifying question-bomb at the class: “Who couldn’t understand my explanation?”

item.title: The Daily Star – Overflow
item.description:
The sound of the rainfall has kept me awake for a while, which to my surprise, I’m not exactly bothered by. After a long day of toiling hard, the last thing I need is something keeping me awake. But the sound of rain keeps striking my ears more as a yearning than a lullaby. Almost as if it’s trying to talk to me. 

I would’ve loved to converse with it if it wasn’t for the terrible migraine knocking at the back of my head like a hammer. This seems a bit annoying. I can feel the pain intensifying itself with each second passing by. 

It’s getting a bit difficult to breathe. What a nuisance! I tried to leave the bed but it felt like my body physically gave up, as if it wanted to drown in that pain instead of mustering up the strength to get up. 

But it’s kind of uncanny. I am in immense pain and I’m exhausted to my bones, but I can still think straight. Sure, I can’t act on my thoughts, but still I can clarify within my mind what I need and what I want to do. That same old battle of preferential treatment between need and want. Why do I want something that I don’t need? Why do I get the feeling nobody will answer me back? But then I thought to myself, if anyone did answer back, I’d be in bigger trouble. I wouldn’t know what to reply back to them. 

I can feel my breathing get a lot heavier. That’s not a good sign. Why the hell did I forget to buy my medicines when I knew this might happen to me? Probably because I worked myself to the bone these couple days. Guess I’ll have to make work with just water. 

*ack* OH GOD! I never knew water could taste this bad! I thought I could simmer the pain in my chest with it, much like filling up a pond with raindrops. But taking a sip almost felt like I was pouring water on a glass which was already full. An overflow. 

What is happening to me? 

Why would nobody answer? Where is everybody anyway? Maybe I should calm down. Yes, calm down. Breathe. 

Breathe? I can’t breathe. I know I should leave my bed, get out of here and try to get some fresh air. But for the love of god, I can’t. I’m not just tired, it feels like my entire body is giving up. I always knew nobody could fill the void inside of me until I myself stopped digging that hole. But now, it feels like I’m full to the brim, maybe more than I needed. 

My head feels like it’s going to explode while the ache inside my chest feels more intense than I could have anticipated. My vision is starting to get blurry, but I’m afraid, too afraid to close my eyes. I’m more afraid of darkness than facing my fears. But my body isn’t listening to me anymore. I’m being engulfed by darkness. 

OH GOD! I’m so scared, I’m so alone. I keep asking them for help, for any kind of response, but do they not hear me? I’m slowly losing the strength to think, let alone talk. I just…I just wish that this pain is enough to make me unconscious. 

But I can still hear, it’s echoing a lot inside my ear, but I can still hear the sound of the droplets. Ahh…that feels so soothing. I can finally feel the pain in my body slowly starting to wither away. Is this nightmare finally ending or am I slowly losing my consciousness? Well, it doesn’t matter anymore. 

I just hope that it keeps raining. 

Aminul Ehsan Anan is a junior year student of Development Studies at University of Dhaka.

item.title: The Daily Star – You remind me of home
item.description:
I walked to school ‘neath silver skies,
past shops where old furniture lies.
each piece asleep in dust and gloom,
still waiting for another room.
From my third-floor classroom high,
I’d watch the world go drifting by.
Nadia Furniture, glowing gold,
a story that I wasn’t told.
I built whole lives with wooden frames,
with velvet chairs and pretty names.
I stitched up homes in amber light,
where ceilings didn’t echo night.
Though seas once roared beneath my feet,
and mountains bowed in hush so sweet,
no land I passed would ask me stay—
each one just let me drift away.
And then came you, and all grew still.
You didn’t try to break or fill.
You held me soft, without demand—
just offered me a place to land.
You didn’t build me walls of stone,
but gave me peace I’d never known.
You were the rhythm in the air,
a kind of quiet, steady care.
You remind me of a place
I used to dream, but couldn’t trace!
not bricks and beams or garden loam,
but just the ache of being home.
The day we said goodbye, I knew
you held me like a map worn through,
one you had traced with every mile,
but couldn’t fold—it held your smile.
I closed my eyes; time fell apart
back to the child with the quiet heart,
back to our fingers, side by side,
across the table, choosing pride,
or love, or peace—or just the grace
of two souls finding one small place.
And it all came down to this:
Perhaps I wasn’t meant to stay
in rooms that time would take away.
Perhaps no roof could quite contain
a heart that danced with joy and pain.
Perhaps I was never meant
to find a home,
Perhaps
I was the home, the shore,
where weary hearts return once more,
when they forget just what they seek
and long for love, though worn and weak.
But if not me,if that’s untrue—
then home, at last, was found in you.


Nishat Anjum, while pursuing a degree in medicine, finds herself perpetually caught between medicine and memoirs, forever returning to questions of identity and the emotional cartography of ordinary life.

item.title: The Daily Star – ‘Hollywood, Ending’ and the pressures of fame
item.description:
“You exchange pieces of yourself for celebrity. Celebrity keeps you working, keeps you paid. Keeps me paid, too,” a reporter tells Kai Laramie in Hollywood, Ending.

“Except once I’ve traded those little pieces of myself, I can’t get them back. They’re not mine anymore,” he replies.

These lines capture the bargain at the centre of John Green’s first novel in nine years and his debut in adult fiction. Two actors in their early 20s discover how easily the pursuit of recognition can blur the line between sharing their lives and losing control of their stories. Juniper Castillo, a former Nickelodeon child star, and Kai, a newcomer to film, are cast opposite Marvel superstar Matthew Malone in an art-house Andy Warhol biopic. When 92 per cent of test-screening respondents rate the film in the top two categories, it has a real chance of finding an audience. Its cast must help make that happen. What interests Green is who gets to write the self that fame produces.

Told from the first-person perspectives of Juniper and Kai, the novel unfolds in four parts, following them from the filming of the biopic through its promotional rollout, premiere and aftermath. Warhol is a fitting subject for the biopic. His fascination with celebrity and images speaks to the novel’s interest in the gap between public identity and private life. Kai and Juniper must perform their roles on screen. They must also perform themselves.

The studio sees a possible romance between the two as another way to sell the film, encouraging speculation faster than either can work out what they feel off camera. Carefully planned social media posts help build a “will they, won’t they” narrative. The publicists who tell them to lean into the chemistry and give fans something to talk about see it as simply part of the job. Even affection becomes material.

Both protagonists have histories of childhood abuse. Kai finds the intrusion that comes with growing attention difficult to navigate. He refers to what happened to him only as “it.” When details of his past leak, he is hailed as a heroic survivor. The studio embraces that image and folds it into the film’s publicity.

Kai sits in windowless conference rooms as a new reporter arrives every seven minutes. They tell him, “You have been very public about this,” as though the fact that people know about his past means he chose to tell them. These encounters show how consent can be quietly distorted: a person is pressured into speaking, then treated as though speaking was always their decision.

The junket chapters become a run of talking points: “Matthew is a legend,” “I love Juniper” and “victims have nothing to be ashamed of.” The phrases are repeated until Kai recognises that, although he believes what he is saying, having to say it so often has begun to feel like a betrayal. The form enacts the theme: sincere words, emptied by repetition, become product. Kai grows increasingly uncomfortable with the idea that other people feel entitled to his story and can decide what it means.

Juniper has grown up in the industry and knows how to work within its demands. She has gone public with her story, handles interviews well and is ambitious and strategic about her image. She also understands the cost. “You don’t have to be an actor for the world to pound away at you, to render you two-dimensional, to villainize or heroize, or do both at once,” she says. “But if you’re an actor, everyone gets a ticket to the show.” The line applies to Kai too. He becomes a figure for other people’s purposes, one they can build up or tear down as they choose. The public feels entitled to watch and judge; the person in the spotlight has little say in the version of themselves that emerges.

We do not need to be movie stars today to feel the pressure to curate our lives online or to wonder how much of ourselves to share. We are conscious of which parts to reveal, which to keep private and how others might respond. The stakes are different in Hollywood, but the desire to have some say in how we are seen is familiar.

Green does not suggest that publicity or self-disclosure is always harmful. Openness can bring connection and meaning. His concern is with an industry that blurs the boundary between private life and publicity, turning personal experiences into commodities and privacy into something people are expected to surrender.

What gets taken is the freedom to be ambiguous: to have a feeling, a past or a self that has not yet become a story. The novel is at its best when it observes rather than resolves, and its observations are the reason to read it.

item.title: The Daily Star – Finding home, identity, and art in ‘Parsa’s Pithas’
item.description:
How do you stay connected to your own culture and roots while living thousands of miles away from home? This is the question at the heart of Sumaiya Matin’s debut children’s book Parsa’s Pithas. Set in Canada, the book tells the heartwarming story of a seven-year-old girl named Parsa who, through making pithas with her mother, is able to learn more about her Bangali roots and traditions while also gaining more confidence in her ability to express herself through her art.

The book opens with the young protagonist frustrated at her inability to draw the “perfect” sky. In dire need of a distraction, Parsa decides to take a break from her school art project to instead help her mother make nakshi pakon pithas for the Bangla New Year. However, as the two begin to make the pithas, Parsa’s frustration returns when she realises that she cannot make pithas as smoothly and intricately as her mother. First struggling to make the right consistency of dough, and then betrayed by the breaking of a toothpick, Parsa struggles with a question that every artist has asked themselves at least once —does art have to be perfect in order to be good?

For Parsa, the answer to this question is found in her mother’s stories about the Bangladeshi women who first made nakshi pakon pithas. Learning about the girls in Bangladesh who made art with whatever they had—rice flower, sticks, stones, and thorns of date palm trees—inspires Parsa to jump over the hurdle of perfectionism and focus her energy and creativity in expressing herself in her own unique way rather than trying to replicate what others are doing.

It is in this intertwining of cultural lessons with a story of a young girl persevering and learning not to give up that Parsa’s Pithas achieves immaculately what every good children’s book sets out to do—act as “mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors” for children around the world.

First introduced by children’s literature scholar, Rudine Sims Bishop, the concept of “mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors” is a metaphor for the different ways in which children can see themselves and the world around them in children’s books. Mirrors signify children seeing their own experiences reflected in the books they read, windows symbolise children learning about different cultures through books, and sliding glass doors refer to children using their imaginations to enter experiences that are different from their own. Bishop argues that all three of these reading experiences are essential to the development of a growing child. What makes Parsa’s Pithas so remarkable is that it is able to do all three of these things at the exact same time.

Written primarily with Bangladeshi diaspora children in mind, the book puts to pages an experience that is not often represented in books or media. Though there are an abundance of Bangladeshi children’s books with representation of Bangladeshi characters, we seldom see books made specifically for children who are learning to navigate their Bangladeshi roots and identity while living away from Bangladesh. Acting as a mirror, the story of Parsa and her mother keeping Bangali traditions alive by celebrating Bangla New Year all the way in Canada allows children of the Bangladeshi diaspora to finally see their own unique experiences and struggles be represented on paper.

Afterall, sometimes to keep a culture alive is to be brave and resourceful enough to make it your own.

item.title: The Daily Star – The courage to speak: The life, ideas, and legacy of Ambassador M. Serajul Islam
item.description:
I have known Ambassador M. Serajul Islam—"Shobuj" to me and his friends—for more than six decades. We were both trained at the Civil Service Academy of Pakistan before he went on to serve Bangladesh in the diplomatic service with distinction, while I diverged and chose a career in the academic and business world of the United States. After his retirement, we talked more frequently, furiously yet respectfully debating everything from politics to the future of Bangladesh.

Ambassador M. Serajul Islam did not choose a life of quiet retirement like most of his colleagues, but instead pursued his passion for writing in areas dear to his heart—democracy, governance, and nation building. He was a student of politics, knowledgeable about various models of governance, and passionate about a Bangladesh free of poverty, with universal economic opportunity within the framework of democracy.

It was painful for Ambassador Islam to see the sacrifices of millions ignored by unscrupulous politicians who made Bangladesh their “business”. These politicians enriched themselves and methodically destroyed every institution from the bureaucracy to the judiciary. They did so with impunity. While most retired diplomats and bureaucrats chose to stay silent, Ambassador Islam chose to challenge the injustices through his weapon of writing. 

Freed from the shackles of government protocol, he wrote extensively on a variety of interrelated subjects: elections, electoral integrity, political legitimacy, governance, democratic resilience, constitutional order, rule of law, state reforms, diplomacy, and geopolitics. He also wrote on Bangladesh's relationship with both small and major powers, including India, China, and the USA.

These writings were not theoretical analysis or “safe” remembrances from his diplomatic days but a hard-nosed critique of what was taking place in his beloved Bangladesh. These writings, mostly in the popular media, were not simple criticisms—they were written by a “Master” who backed up his reasoning with logic and provided alternatives drawn from his experiences around the world.

The writings gathered here, carefully selected by his children from hundreds of published materials, provide readers with a glimpse of who he was: an uncompromising patriot and champion of freedom and democracy. This is not one of those books you read once and then leave as an untouched decoration on the bookshelf. Instead, most readers will read it again and again, finding parallels with issues of the present.

Ambassador Serajul Islam's arguments for democracy are timeless, and his ideas about good governance are proven models drawn from the best practices around the world. His advocacy for the “have-nots” reflects who he was as a person, and his courageous voice for equal protection for everyone before the judiciary speaks to his upbringing and values.

Readers should also recall that Ambassador Islam was writing courageously when the rights of Bangladeshis were being systematically taken away and Bangladesh was becoming a sub-contractor—politically and economically—to India. He was threatened directly and indirectly but could not be silenced. Sadly, he passed away within days of the student-led revolution which toppled the autocratic regime. Both the interim government and the current elected government would have benefited a great deal from Ambassador M. Serajul Islam's advice and guidance.

Through his writings, Ambassador Islam has left behind a body of work which should be read by researchers and policymakers alike. His writings include some of the most sensitive subjects in Bangladesh’s recent history—the relationship between Bangladesh and India, the role of US Ambassadors in Bangladeshi politics, the breakdown of law and order including deliberate misinterpretation of the constitution, and China's master-class diplomacy. Concurrently, he wrote about a potential and doable path for Bangladesh to secure its own future.

Ambassador Islam passionately believed that a nation of 180 million people should chart its own path, maintaining good but never subservient relationships with global powers. He was acutely aware of “our traits as a nation” but remained firm in his belief that the country could only thrive under Lincoln's doctrine of government “of the people, by the people, and for the people.”

Ambassador M. Serajul Islam’s testimony at the Dhaka Forum in October 2018: “Bangladesh is the only country in modern history whose people have sacrificed their lives by the millions to establish a country where they should be able to express their opinions without fear and elect the government of their choice in a free and fair national election,” echoes throughout his writings and is his fitting epitaph.

Dr. Faisal M. Rahman, Founding Dean & Professor, The Graham School of Management, Saint Xavier University, Chicago, USA. Dr. Rahman is also President of the APAC Group of healthcare companies. Contact: [email protected]
